title: As Far From the Land as Possible

concept.title: A multi-source BFS from the land: the last layer is the farthest water cell
body: On a map with land (`1`) and water (`0`), the distance between two cells is the number of steps up, down, left and right (on this open grid it is the Manhattan distance, with no obstacles in the way). Find a water cell whose distance to the **nearest** land cell is **as large as possible**, and print that distance. If there is no land, or no water, print -1.

This is the multi-source search of the nearest-zero task with the roles named differently: start with **all land cells** in the first layer; each layer is one step farther from the land. The layer number in which the **last** water cell is reached is the largest distance of any water cell to the land.
Counting layers needs care with the first layer (distance 0, the land itself): the answer is the index of the last layer that was not empty. The time is O(h * w).

statement: A map has `h` rows and `w` columns of land (`1`) and water (`0`). For a water cell, its distance to the land is the smallest number of steps (up, down, left, right, over any cells) to a land cell. Print the largest such distance over all water cells, or -1 if the map has no land or no water.
inputFormat: The first line has `h` and `w`: the number of rows and columns.
Each of the next `h` lines has a row of `w` characters.

examples.note: The cell in the opposite corner is 4 steps away from the only land cell: 4.

hints: Start a search from all land cells together.
Each layer is one step farther from the land; count the layers.
If the map has no land or no water, print -1.

solution.complexity: Time O(h * w), space O(h * w).
